findings.description: AWS access key ID and secret access key are hard-coded in plaintext within the EC2 user_data script, which is accessible via the instance metadata service, EC2 describe-instance-attribute API, and Terraform state. This exposes long-lived IAM credentials to anyone with access to any of these.
Ingress rule allows SSH (port 22) from 0.0.0.0/0, exposing administrative access to the entire internet and enabling brute-force or credential-stuffing attacks.
Ingress rule allows HTTP (port 80) from 0.0.0.0/0 with no corresponding HTTPS listener or TLS termination, exposing web traffic to the public internet in cleartext and enabling interception.

Egress rule allows all traffic (protocol -1, all ports) to 0.0.0.0/0, providing no network egress restriction and increasing the impact of a compromised instance, such as data exfiltration or command-and-control callbacks.

map_public_ip_on_launch is set to true, automatically assigning public IPs to instances launched in this subnet, which directly increases internet exposure for the portal_server instance that also has SSH and HTTP open to the world.
map_public_ip_on_launch is set to true, automatically assigning public IPs to any instance launched in this subnet, expanding the network attack surface unnecessarily.
The EBS volume does not set encrypted = true, leaving data stored on this volume unencrypted at rest.

The S3 bucket used to store VPC flow logs has no server-side encryption configuration (no aws_s3_bucket_server_side_encryption_configuration), leaving potentially sensitive network traffic metadata unencrypted at rest.

The S3 bucket has no public access block, bucket policy, or ACL restricting access, and force_destroy is enabled, leaving it potentially open to misconfiguration-driven public exposure of flow log data.
